To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the FMR1 premutation and full mutation are stable in cultured fetal fibroblastic cell lines and (2) the FMRP protein is present and is stable in the cell lines from the full mutation.

(1) the expression of the fragile X full mutation in human fibroblasts and in the mouse model of the disorder (the Fmr1 knockout mouse) is dynamic; (2) the dynamic expression of the fragile full mutation in fibroblasts is due to a change in the methylation status of the FMR1 promoter, and (3) the dynamic expression in the mouse model is due to a decrease in the level of the transcriptional regulator, CTCF.

1) a significant number of patients with a clinical diagnosis of FXTAS have normal CGG repeat lengths; 2) FXTAS patients with normal CGG repeat sizes have a significantly increased risk for the development of FXTAS; and 3) a significant number FXTAS patients have premutations that are associated with a significantly increased risk of developing FXTAS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new and efficient methods of analysis of the dynamic behavior of the fragile X full mutation.
the study of the molecular basis for the pathogenesis of the fragile X syndrome and the development of a mouse model of the disorder.
the development of a method of analysis for dynamic behavior of the fragile X full mutation in cultured female fibroblasts using the polymerase chain reaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence that the presence of the FMR1 gene in the human genome has been the result of a horizontal gene transfer event.

the dynamic behavior of the FMR1 CGG-repeat expansion in cultured female fetal skin fibroblasts is a complex and dynamic process that involves the formation of a variety of repeat structures that are in dynamic equilibrium with one another and with the surrounding genomic DNA.

the use of the term “fragile X syndrome” is appropriate for all cases with a mutation in the FMR1 gene, including those with premutation alleles, and that the use of “fragile X mental retardation” or “fragile X-associated mental retardation” is inappropriate for all cases with an FMR1 mutation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expression of the FMR1 gene is regulated at the level of transcription and translation.
the FMR1 gene is a fragile site that is subject to a variety of mutational processes that include deletions and expansions.
we are trying to understand how the fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) regulates the translation and/or stability of mRNAs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dynamic behavior of fragile X syndrome full mutations in cultured fibroblasts is similar to that observed in the brains of affected individuals.
the fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) is a dynamic protein, with a half-life of 2-3 hours in cultured cells.
the fragile X syndrome (FXS) is a complex disease that is influenced by many factors, including genetic and environmental factors.
